hero.h1: From a rack to an atom. 800 million times closer.
hero.lede: Zoom into a real AI chip, level by level. At every level, explore how it works, build something, break it, or imagine what comes next.
hero.map.label: Die view
hero.map.note: This die is also the map of the lab: each block is one layer you can explore, and some zoom further down. Pick a block.
hero.gate.label: Gate
hero.gate.note: Off: the gate squeezes all three sheets shut, so no current flows. Older, flat transistors still leaked here.
hero.hook.1: 72 GPUs, cabled so they act like one giant computer.
hero.hook.2: Liquid, not air: cold plates carry the heat off every chip.
hero.hook.3: 336 billion transistors and 288 GB of memory in one package.
hero.hook.4: As big as one flash of light can print: about 26 × 33 mm.
hero.hook.5: Tensor cores do almost all of the AI math.
hero.hook.6: Every gate is a ready-made cell, wired on stacked copper layers.
hero.hook.8: Three sheets about 5 nm thick, gripped on every side.
hero.hook.9: Only about 20 atoms thick. That is why shrinking is so hard.
hero.why.1.build: A rack exists to answer questions cheaply. Design the chip that does it.
hero.why.1.break: At this scale, one chip in thousands quietly giving wrong answers becomes a daily problem.
hero.why.1.imagine: The future of AI may be decided by electricity as much as by chips.
hero.why.2.build: One tray holds several kinds of chip, each picked for a different job.
hero.why.2.break: Every part on this board crossed borders to get here. Break one link.
hero.why.2.imagine: New chips start as companies. Can yours reach first silicon?
hero.why.3.build: Pick the dies, memory stacks and package for the biggest chip you can make.
hero.why.3.break: Two dies and eight memory stacks: one bad part can waste the whole package.
hero.why.3.imagine: What if the whole model lived on one giant wafer instead of in memory stacks?
hero.why.4.build: Your own design can end up on a real die, on a shared community chip.
hero.why.4.break: Every die is tested before it ships. How much testing is enough?
hero.why.4.imagine: Does the future even look like this die?
hero.why.5.build: Add your own instruction to a real open processor. That is how AI chips begin.
hero.why.5.break: AI now helps design blocks like this one. Can you tell when it is wrong?
hero.why.5.imagine: What if the math happened inside the memory, with no data moving at all?
hero.why.6.build: Place and wire your own cells. Too tight and the wires no longer fit.
hero.why.6.break: Signals take time to cross these wires. Push the clock until it breaks.
hero.why.6.imagine: Blind evolution sometimes finds circuits no engineer would draw.
hero.why.7.build: Cells like this one become the processor you program later.
hero.why.7.break: One wrong connection in one cell, copied a billion times.
hero.why.7.imagine: Could a machine design the cells themselves?
hero.why.8.build: Try the gate switch on the picture first: on, current flows; off, it should stop completely.
hero.why.8.break: No two of these switches are exactly alike, and they wear out with use.
hero.why.8.imagine: CFET stacks the two kinds of switch on top of each other. 2D materials may come after that.
hero.why.9.build: Every chip starts as one flawless crystal. Grow it yourself.
hero.why.9.break: Physics sets a minimum energy for every bit. Try to cheat it.
hero.why.9.imagine: Today we are far above the floor. How close could a future machine get?

map.aboutText: Open Silicon Lab is an open-source project about every kind of chip, from the microcontroller in a thermostat to the GPUs in an AI data center. It is made with AI: Claude wrote the text, simulations and code with the project owner, from public sources. Every simulation is a teaching model; each one says what it simplifies. Facts carry their source and the date they were last verified, and are rechecked every month.

wi.simplifiesText: A teaching model, not a forecast. Each rule says which way one thing pushes another, and the directions follow the economics and the events of 2021–2026 below. The strengths are illustrative round numbers. The real industry has delays, feedback loops (higher prices cool demand; shortages pay for new fabs that later end them), stockpiles, contracts and politics, which this model leaves out. Effects are shown as changes from today, all at once.

cz.tipCell: Select a cell to open it at the next level.
cz.tipFet: Select a transistor to zoom into it.
cz.tipFlop: That is a flip-flop: it holds one bit between clock ticks. Memory and the clock shows what is inside one.
cz.shape.180: a flat (planar) transistor with a polysilicon gate
cz.shape.130: a flat (planar) transistor with a polysilicon gate
cz.shape.28: a flat (planar) transistor with a metal gate on a high-k insulator
cz.shape.3: stacked silicon sheets with the gate wrapped all around them
cz.level.board.name: Demo board
cz.level.board.d: A demo board like Tiny Tapeout's: switches set your chip's inputs and LEDs show its outputs. A small helper microcontroller picks which design on the shared chip is switched on.
cz.level.pkg.name: Package
cz.level.pkg.d: With the lid off: thin gold bond wires join the pads around the edge of the silicon die to the package's pins, which are soldered to the board.
cz.level.die.name: Shared chip
cz.level.die.d: One die shared by {tiles} tiles, each a different person's design. Yours is the outlined one. Sharing the masks is what makes a chip cost a few hundred dollars instead of millions.
cz.level.die.d28: Commercial shuttles share one die between many {node} designs too, but a slot costs far more and the design kits are not open. Yours is the outlined one.
cz.level.die.d3: At 3 nm there are no shared shuttles like this: only companies that pay for a whole mask set make chips. This shows where your design would sit if there were one.
cz.level.tile.name: Your tile
cz.level.tile.d: Your tile is about {tw} × {th} µm at {node}. Your design, {cells} cells in {w} × {h} µm, fills about {share}% of it: there is room for far more.
cz.level.design.name: Your design
cz.level.design.d: {cells} standard cells placed in rows by simulated annealing, joined by {wires} µm of wire on two metal layers with {vias} vias between them. Bright wires carry a 1, dark ones a 0.
cz.level.cell.name: One cell
cz.level.cell.d: Your {type} cell opened up: {n} transistors. The p-type ones on top connect the output to 1, the n-type ones below connect it to 0, and the inputs make sure exactly one side conducts.
cz.level.fet.name: One transistor
cz.level.fet.d: This {kind} in your cell is {state}. At {node} it is {shape}; its gate is roughly {len} long. The voltage on the gate opens or closes the channel between source and drain.
cz.note: Built from your design with the same engines as the labs: the cells, their places, the wires and every value on them are computed, and the tests check that each cell's transistors give the same answer as its logic. Simplified: the board, package and shared chip are drawn in general terms (a Tiny Tapeout-style chip of 160 tiles; tiles drawn at Tiny Tapeout's SKY130 size, scaled with the process), a cell is drawn as its circuit inside its real outline rather than as its masks, and the transistor is a sketch, not to scale in depth.

zoom.1.name: AI rack
zoom.1.d: A rack-scale AI system in the class of NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72: 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs on trays, cabled so they behave like one giant computer. Liquid cooling pipes run down each side. Shipping from the second half of 2026.
zoom.2.name: Compute tray
zoom.2.d: One slide-out tray seen from above. GPU packages, a CPU, its memory, power stages and connectors sit on a circuit board under liquid-cooled cold plates.
zoom.3.name: GPU package
zoom.3.d: Two reticle-size compute dies sit side by side on a silicon interposer, flanked by eight HBM4 memory stacks. The whole package holds 336 billion transistors and 288 GB of memory.
zoom.4.name: Compute die
zoom.4.d: One die is about 26 × 33 mm, the largest area a scanner can print in one exposure. It is tiled with identical processor blocks (streaming multiprocessors) around a shared cache band.
zoom.5.name: Streaming multiprocessor
zoom.5.d: One processor block, about 3 mm across. Amber blocks are tensor cores, the matrix engines that do almost all AI math. Cyan banks are register files; the violet band is fast on-chip SRAM.
zoom.6.name: Standard-cell rows
zoom.6.d: Logic is laid out as rows of standard cells, each a pre-designed gate such as NAND or a flip-flop. The colored lines are copper wires on stacked metal layers that connect them.
zoom.7.name: One logic cell
zoom.7.d: A cell as a layout engineer sees it. Red vertical lines are gates about 48 nm apart. Green strips are transistor channels (p-type above, n-type below). Grey rails carry power.
zoom.8.name: Nanosheet transistor
zoom.8.d: A cut through one gate-all-around transistor: three silicon nanosheets, each about 5 nm thick, fully wrapped by the gate metal (amber) and a thin insulator (violet). Electrons flow from source to drain when the gate is on.
zoom.9.name: Silicon atoms
zoom.9.d: The channel is a silicon crystal with atoms 0.235 nm apart. A 5 nm nanosheet is only about 20 atoms thick, which is why further shrinking is so hard and new materials are being studied.

dv.note: Prototype (docs/FRAME.md). The adder, its cells, wires and transistors are computed by the same engines as the tiny-chip studio, at the process this lab models nearest the year (180, 130, 28 or 3 nm). Everything above the chip is drawn in general terms. Figures come from the lab's checked facts.
dv.d.building: A data centre: long halls of racks, pumps and cooling, with its own substation to feed them.
dv.d.rack: One rack: trays of GPUs wired together so tightly they work like one giant chip, cooled by water.
dv.d.board: One tray: GPUs, a CPU and memory on one board. Numbers stream out of memory into the GPUs, over and over.
dv.d.chip: One GPU package: compute dies side by side, ringed by stacks of memory. Each die is a grid of cores: orange for arithmetic, teal for memory.
dv.d.block: Inside one core: a grid of multiply-add units passing numbers to each other. In one of them sits an adder, drawn as its real cells and wires at {node}.
dv.d.gate: One cell of that adder, opened up. Each transistor is a switch; together they turn the bits coming in into the bit going out. Bright wires carry a 1.
dv.d.switch: One transistor. A voltage on the gate opens a channel under it, and electrons rush from source to drain. Take the voltage away and the channel closes.
dv.d.atom: The channel, atom by atom. It is only a few dozen atoms long, so electrons can sometimes slip straight through even when the switch is off.

dv.t.building.1947: 1947: ENIAC fills a room with about 18,000 vacuum tubes. It computes artillery tables, not answers to questions.
dv.t.building.1964: 1964: the mainframe era. One computer room serves a whole company, through punched cards and terminals.
dv.t.building.1995: 1995: server rooms grow with the web. Each server sends out web pages.
dv.t.building.2006: 2006: warehouse-scale data centres: tens of thousands of identical servers run as one computer.
dv.t.building.2023: Since 2023: AI halls. Racks so hot that water pipes run to every chip, and the site needs a substation.
dv.t.building.2027: Unfinished: power plants planned beside data centres. Where the electricity will come from is still open.
dv.t.rack.1947: 1947: ENIAC's panels: racks of vacuum tubes, programmed by moving cables by hand.
dv.t.rack.1964: 1964: mainframe cabinets: tape drives, blinking lights and memory made of tiny magnetic rings.
dv.t.rack.1995: 1995: rack-mounted servers: dozens of thin computers stacked in one cabinet.
dv.t.rack.2016: 2016: GPU servers: eight GPUs in a box, built for training neural networks.
dv.t.rack.2024: Since 2024: racks of 72 GPUs joined through a copper backplane so they act as one, cooled by liquid.
dv.t.rack.2027: Unfinished: light instead of copper between the chips, and racks that need ever more power and cooling.
dv.t.board.before: Not yet: until 1971 there is no processor on a single chip to put on a board.
dv.t.board.1971: 1971: the first microprocessor. A whole processor on one chip, on a board with a few memory chips.
dv.t.board.1999: 1999: the GPU arrives on graphics cards, ringed by its own fast memory chips.
dv.t.board.2016: 2016: stacked memory (HBM) moves right beside the GPU, inside the same package.
dv.t.board.2026: Today: compute trays with GPUs, a CPU and stacks of HBM4 memory, cooled by liquid plates.
dv.t.board.2027: Unfinished: memory and compute pressed ever closer. Should they become one thing?
dv.t.chip.before: Not yet: until 1959 there are no integrated circuits. Every transistor is a separate part.
dv.t.chip.1959: 1959: the first integrated circuits: a few transistors on one piece of silicon.
dv.t.chip.1971: {year}: the biggest chip so far is the {chip}, with {n} transistors.
dv.t.chip.2027: Unfinished: if the trend of the biggest AI chips held, one would hold about {n} transistors in {year}. A trend line, not a forecast.
dv.t.block.before: Not yet: until 1971 no single chip can do arithmetic on its own.
dv.t.block.1971: 1971: an adder that works on four bits at a time, at the heart of the first microprocessor.
dv.t.block.2006: 2006: several cores per chip, each with its own adders and multipliers.
dv.t.block.2017: Since 2017: tensor cores, grids of multiply-add units built just for AI.
dv.t.block.2027: Unfinished: computing inside the memory, or with light? The grid may not stay a grid.
dv.t.gate.before: Not yet: CMOS, the pairing of switches drawn here, is invented in 1963. Until then logic is built from vacuum tubes, relays and single transistors.
dv.t.gate.1963: 1963: CMOS is invented: one set of switches pulls the output up, its mirror pulls it down, and almost no power is wasted while waiting.
dv.t.gate.1985: Since 1985: CMOS is everywhere. Nearly every logic gate in the world is built like this one.
dv.t.gate.2027: Unfinished: gates that compute with light, with chance, or that never erase a bit.
dv.t.switch.1947: 1947: the first transistor, at Bell Labs: two gold contacts pressed onto a crystal of germanium.
dv.t.switch.1959: 1959: the MOS transistor: a flat switch with its gate laid on top of the silicon.
dv.t.switch.2011: 2011: FinFET: the channel stands up as a thin fin, and the gate wraps three sides of it.
dv.t.switch.2022: Since 2022: gate-all-around nanosheets: the gate surrounds stacked silicon sheets on every side.
dv.t.switch.2033: Projection: CFET, n-type and p-type switches stacked on top of each other (imec's roadmap). Not built yet.
dv.t.atom.1947: 1947: the first transistors are made of germanium, not silicon.
dv.t.atom.1954: 1954: the first silicon transistor. Silicon wins: it keeps working when warm and grows a near-perfect insulating skin.
dv.t.atom.2007: 2007: the insulator under the gate is only a few atoms thick, so new materials (high-k) replace it to stop the leaks.
dv.t.atom.2022: Today: a gate spans a few dozen silicon atoms. Every atom out of place matters.
dv.t.atom.2027: Unfinished: channels made of materials one atom thick (2D materials), on imec's roadmap for around 2043.
dv.e.over-horizon.q: Almost every advanced chip comes from a few places. Why can't the know-how simply be written down and copied?
dv.e.over-horizon.try: New fabs in the US, Japan and Europe, training thousands of engineers, and AI that learns from a factory's own data.
dv.e.power-next-door.place: A power line still being drawn
dv.e.power-next-door.q: Each word of an answer costs less energy every year, yet we ask for ever more. Can the planet afford the answers we want?
dv.e.power-next-door.try: Liquid cooling, building next to power plants, more work per joule, and new deals for nuclear, wind and solar power.
dv.e.twenty-watts.q: A brain answers questions on about the power of a dim light bulb. What would we copy from it?
dv.e.twenty-watts.try: Neuromorphic chips with spiking neurons, computing inside memory, and chips that copy the brain's wiring.
dv.e.one-mind.q: How do 72 chips share one answer without waiting on each other?
dv.e.one-mind.try: Copper links that join every GPU to every other, and light for the longer distances.
dv.e.rack-shape.place: The empty space at the top
dv.e.rack-shape.q: Who decides how a rack is built, and what happens when the designs are open to everyone?
dv.e.rack-shape.try: The Open Compute Project publishes rack, power and server designs that anyone can build and improve.
dv.e.memory-wall.place: The road between memory and chip
dv.e.memory-wall.q: The chip often sits waiting for its numbers to arrive. Should memory and compute stay apart at all?
dv.e.memory-wall.try: Stacking memory right beside the chip (HBM), wider and faster stacks, and computing inside the memory.
dv.e.silent-errors.q: With hundreds of billions of switches, a few will go wrong without telling anyone. How do you trust the answer?
dv.e.silent-errors.try: Testing chips while they work, running work twice, and designs that check their own results.
dv.e.reticle-seam.q: A chip can only be printed so big. If we invented chipmaking today, would we still print it in pieces?
dv.e.reticle-seam.try: Joining dies side by side in one package (chiplets), chips as big as a whole wafer, and packaging on square panels.
dv.e.where-it-thinks.q: Billions of tiny additions make one sentence. Where, in all this arithmetic, does the thinking happen?
dv.e.where-it-thinks.try: Systolic arrays that pass numbers from unit to unit, so each number is fetched from memory only once.
dv.e.empty-slot.place: An empty unit in the grid
dv.e.empty-slot.q: This slot could hold a block someone imagined. How could your idea become part of a chip?
dv.e.empty-slot.try: Open design tools, shared chip runs such as Tiny Tapeout, and AI agents that help write and check designs.
dv.e.not-electric.place: A wire that could carry light
dv.e.not-electric.q: Must a switch be electrical at all? What is the strangest thing that could compute?
dv.e.not-electric.try: Light steered through tiny interferometers, bits that flip by chance (p-bits), and living neurons on a chip.
dv.e.erasing-costs.place: The bit that gets thrown away
dv.e.erasing-costs.q: Each time this gate forgets an input, physics charges a tiny cost in heat. Could a computer never forget?
dv.e.erasing-costs.try: Reversible logic that recycles its energy, and chips that run closer to the physical limit.
dv.e.after-nanosheet.q: Flat, then fins, then sheets. What comes after the nanosheet, and can anything keep doubling forever?
dv.e.after-nanosheet.try: Stacking the n- and p-type switches on top of each other (CFET), and channels one atom thick.
dv.e.no-atoms-left.q: When a gate is a few atoms long, there is little left to shrink. What could a chip never do?
dv.e.no-atoms-left.try: New materials, new kinds of switch, and finding the physics floor for every operation.
dv.e.atom-by-atom.q: Films are laid one atomic layer at a time, in a thousand steps or more. Could a chip be built atom by atom?
dv.e.atom-by-atom.try: Depositing and etching one atomic layer at a time, and research tools that place single atoms.
dv.q.strange: What is the strangest thing that could compute?
dv.q.limit: What could a chip never do, and could it learn to?
dv.q.fail: Why can a perfect design fail in the real world?
dv.q.idea: How could your idea become a chip?
dv.q.make: What would chipmaking look like if we invented it from scratch today?
dv.q.know: What part of making chips can't be written down?
dv.q.open: What happens when anyone can make a chip?
dv.q.divide: How should a chip divide its work?
dv.q.life: What new kinds of computers could brains, swarms and living cells inspire?
dv.q.scale: What will be the next Moore's law?
